subject: environmental-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Soil can be regarded as a system because it:
options: Is completely closed to the environment
Has inputs, outputs, stores and flows of energy and matter
questions.explain: Soil is an open system with inputs (litter, rain), outputs (leaching, erosion), and internal stores and flows.

questions.q: A temperature inversion worsens urban smog because it:
options: Increases wind speed and disperses pollutants
Traps a layer of cool air and pollutants near the ground
questions.explain: An inversion places warm air above cooler surface air, preventing vertical mixing so pollutants accumulate near the ground.

questions.q: A high BOD value in a river generally indicates:
options: High levels of organic pollution and low oxygen availability
questions.explain: High BOD means a lot of organic pollution, so microbes consume oxygen, leaving little for other life.

questions.q: Crop rotation helps maintain soil fertility chiefly by:
options: Varying nutrient demands and including legumes that fix nitrogen
questions.explain: Rotating crops, including nitrogen-fixing legumes, replenishes nutrients and reduces pest build-up.

questions.q: BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) measures:
options: The oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter
The pH of a water body
The total nitrate concentration of water
questions.explain: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen used by microbes breaking down organic matter in water.

questions.q: Which is a feature of more sustainable agriculture?
options: Heavy reliance on synthetic inputs and monoculture
Integrated pest management and maintaining soil organic matter
Maximising short-term yield regardless of soil loss
questions.explain: Sustainable farming uses methods like IPM, rotation and organic matter management to protect long-term productivity.

questions.q: Economic water scarcity, in contrast, results mainly from:
options: A genuine lack of freshwater resources
Lack of investment and infrastructure to access available water
questions.explain: Economic scarcity occurs where water exists but poverty or poor infrastructure prevents its use.

questions.q: Which best sequences the eutrophication process?
options: Nutrient input, algal bloom, light blocked, decomposition, oxygen depletion
Oxygen rises, algae die, fish thrive
Acid rain, fish death, algal recovery
questions.explain: Nutrients fuel algal blooms that block light; their decay by bacteria then depletes dissolved oxygen.

questions.q: A property that made CFCs commercially attractive but environmentally harmful was that they are:
options: Heavier than air so they sink
Water soluble and easily washed out
questions.explain: CFCs are very stable and unreactive, so they persist long enough to reach the stratosphere where UV breaks them apart.

questions.q: Substitutes introduced to replace CFCs, such as HCFCs and HFCs, were chosen mainly because they:
options: Have no effect on climate at all
Are cheaper to produce than anything else
Cause less or no stratospheric ozone depletion
questions.explain: HCFCs and HFCs were adopted to reduce or eliminate ozone depletion, though some are still potent greenhouse gases.

questions.q: Secondary treatment in wastewater management mainly involves:
options: Microbial breakdown of dissolved organic matter to lower BOD
questions.explain: Secondary treatment uses microbes to digest dissolved organics, substantially reducing the effluent's BOD.

questions.q: During the hydrological cycle, the process by which water vapour returns to liquid is:
questions.explain: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid droplets, forming clouds.

questions.q: Ground-level ozone is considered harmful, whereas stratospheric ozone is beneficial. This illustrates that ozone is:
options: Beneficial or harmful depending on its location in the atmosphere
questions.explain: The same molecule protects life as a stratospheric UV shield but acts as a harmful pollutant at ground level.

questions.q: A loam soil is generally considered ideal for agriculture because it:
options: Balances sand, silt and clay for good drainage and nutrient retention
Is pure clay that drains poorly
Is pure sand with no nutrients
questions.explain: Loam mixes sand, silt and clay, giving good drainage, aeration and nutrient/water retention.

questions.q: Which practice best conserves soil on sloping farmland?
options: Ploughing straight up and down the slope
questions.explain: Contour ploughing and terracing slow water flow across slopes, reducing runoff and soil erosion.

questions.q: In the DPSIR framework, what does the 'P' stand for?
questions.explain: DPSIR stands for Drivers, Pressures, State, Impact and Response.

questions.q: Wind and water removing fertile topsoil from bare land is an example of:
questions.explain: Soil erosion is the physical removal of topsoil by wind or water, especially where vegetation is absent.

questions.q: A key environmental drawback of intensive (industrial) agriculture is:
options: High inputs of fertiliser and pesticide causing pollution
questions.explain: Intensive farming raises yields but heavy agrochemical and fossil-fuel inputs cause pollution and habitat loss.

questions.q: Salinisation of soil, common in irrigated drylands, occurs when:
options: Evaporation draws salts to the surface where they accumulate
questions.explain: In hot climates irrigation water evaporates, leaving dissolved salts that build up and harm crops.

questions.q: Indicator species such as stonefly larvae are used to assess water quality because they:
options: Are sensitive to pollution and require clean, oxygen-rich water
Survive only in polluted, low-oxygen water
Are found only in the sea
questions.explain: Pollution-sensitive species like stonefly larvae thrive only in clean, well-oxygenated water, signalling good quality.

questions.q: 'Food miles' refer to the:
options: Amount of fertiliser used per hectare
Distance food travels from production to consumer
questions.explain: Food miles measure the transport distance of food, an indicator (though imperfect) of associated emissions.

questions.q: Which of the following would be classed as the 'State' in the DPSIR framework?
options: The measured air-quality or pollutant concentration
questions.explain: State refers to the current condition of the environment, such as measured pollutant concentrations.

questions.q: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have:
options: Physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food
Access to fish but not crops
questions.explain: Food security means reliable physical and economic access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active life.

questions.q: Compared with sandy soil, clay soil typically has:
options: Smaller particles, higher water retention and poorer drainage
questions.explain: Clay has tiny particles that hold water and nutrients but drain slowly and can become waterlogged.

questions.q: Over-abstraction of groundwater from an aquifer can lead to:
options: Falling water tables and, near coasts, saltwater intrusion
questions.explain: Pumping faster than recharge lowers water tables and can draw saline seawater into coastal aquifers.

questions.q: In the DPSIR framework, a 'Driver' would best be described as:
options: The measured change in environmental quality
A management policy introduced by government
The underlying human need or activity such as demand for energy
questions.explain: Drivers are the fundamental social and economic forces, such as energy demand, that lead to environmental pressures.

questions.q: Compared with terrestrial systems, aquatic food production (fishing) differs in that humans largely:
options: Harvest from higher trophic levels of wild populations
questions.explain: Capture fisheries mostly take wild secondary or tertiary consumers, unlike terrestrial farming of producers.

questions.q: Reducing speed limits and promoting public transport to cut vehicle emissions is pollution management by:
options: Altering the human activity producing pollution
questions.explain: Changing how and how much people drive tackles pollution at the activity level before pollutants are produced.

questions.q: Primary productivity in aquatic systems is often limited by light and by the availability of:
options: Nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate
questions.explain: Aquatic primary productivity is commonly limited by nutrients, especially nitrate and phosphate, plus light.

questions.q: A major source of the nitrate and phosphate that cause eutrophication is:
options: Runoff of fertilisers and sewage from land
questions.explain: Agricultural fertiliser runoff and sewage are leading sources of the nutrients driving eutrophication.
